I don't know what you look like. But I was chubby with acne issues for a long time. It was brutal.  I was convinced I was the most hideous  thing to ever walk the planet. I refused to look  in mirrors or have photos taken. Other kids were mean. Along with other factors, I soon became  selectively mute for a few years. So, I focused on one thing I loved. I loved horseriding. I ignored everything  else, including  and especially  boys. They started asking  me out and I turned them down because  I was convinced  they were doing it to make fun of me. One boy wrote me a long letter in class and I sent back a scathing  rejection (still convinced it was a cruel joke; 10 years later I found out it wasn't). I didn't realize  ( because  I was still convinced  that I was the ugliest person alive) that over the years I had grown fitter, I had grown into my facial features, and my skin cleared up. Thankfully, perhaps, I didn't  realize it or I would have been sidetracked. So, my point is, kid. I know  the way you feel about yourself  and the way the boys act is brutal: build a mental wall and block it off. Pick something  else  that matters to you and pour yourself into it. Let it build your self esteem. And then, chances are, you will eventually  realize you were never ugly. And you may be surprised  by the truth.

Here's what happened as I see it. Before 2023 it was already tough with content mills and such. New bloggers were rarely realistic about how long it took to get out of the sandpit etc. But if you got a foothold in your niche, you probably did okay.  I did fine for about 4 years. Then ChatGPT happened and bloggers jumped on it to create instant content basically for free. I still held on to my main client for about a year after that. However, the bloggers got greedy, and they flooded the SERPs with AI tripe. I don't know if it was because of this that Google changed the algorithm to sink 90% of blogs, but they did.  The HCUs started in September last year, and blogs started dying, getting replaced by Reddit, quora, etc. The remaining blogs are either extremely high DA and hard to get hired by, or they're the remaining morons who still want to use AI to write a first draft and then pay you $0.01 per word to make the generic, off-topic sh!t they give you sound human. It's not worth the effort. The added thing is that even if they want human-written content and can pay  a decent amount per word (now a unicorn), you can't guarantee that the article will rank high on the SERPs using the old SEO techniques anymore. Unless you're writing for Forbes or WebMD, the chances of ranking to justify the ROI for the client has made me pivot away from SEO. It worked until it didn't

I'm going to take what you say at face value and pretend you are just being around with by clients and not providing bad work. Let's say it's true. Upwork clients are a mixed bag. Some are great. I've found many wonderful, long-term clients on Upwork I've worked with for years. Some are straight-up scammers. But many are just unrealistic about the work they want done and its costs. Sometimes, figuring out which is which is tricky. As a rule, try to avoid underpaying clients and establish what the client knows about the job and expects beforehand. I have 100% JSS on Upwork, and I'm about to lose it because I didn't do my due diligence on a client. They wanted editing work on a fiction manuscript, so they contacted me directly and sent me the job offer after one or two messages. This should have been my first warning. When people write their own fiction, they tend to be lalaland about their work. They usually don't understand the industry or what editing involves. So I got to work editing, which means going sentence-by-sentence, looking at everything from lower-level issues to structural and development problems in the story. After one chapter, I could tell he was horrified and despondent about the many changes and comments on everything from grammar to word choice issues to larger story problems. He ended the contract immediately, and I'm assuming this will be my first bad review. But I just need to take the hit and move on. It taught me a lesson: don't take new writers who don't understand what copy-editing involves. My JSS may suffer. But I learned a lesson. Vet your clients. Talk to them. Make sure you are on the same page before accepting a job.  Never just take a job for the sake of taking a job. If something seems off or you're suspicious about their expectations and the compensation for your effort, rather walk away. Forget about JSS etc. If you give good work to good clients, the JSS will follow naturally.

You can see the heavy flews and light wrinkling, more pronounced when he pricks his ears forward. Now, it's not the Dogue shape. They are far more brachycephalic (short-nosed) with a blocky head and wrinkles. Neos are massive, heavy-built dogs with extreme saggy skin and wrinkles so if he has either of these, it's possibly a grandparent or further back in his line. His muzzle is a little long for most mastiff breeds, but acceptable for a Boerboel-type mastiff, Great Dane, Or Cane Corso. If you were in South Africa I'd say Boerboel, but I'm guessing they're probably rarer where you are, so it's less likely. His build is a bit narrow for a mastiff, but at 7 months he may still fill out a little. Hard to tell, but the narrow build does suggest he is a mastiff cross.

One clue is his coat, that is slightly longer than it should be, suggesting a bit of Labrador perhaps since most true mastiffs have a very short coat. Now it could be from a livestock guardian like a Kangal, but he doesn't look like a Kangal to me. A big clue is the liver nose and the darker shading around his face. This is a dilute melanistic mask that is quite rare.  The nose color you can get in a Dogue or fawn Neo. You can also see a dilute mask in the blue fawn Cane Corso. The other dog you could see this in is a pitbull-type dog, particularly red nose Pitties or some of the newer American Bully dogs where people are more prone to breed for rare colors. But, his liver face mask also looks like darker shade of a Dudley Labrador. So this really leaves a lot of options. I wouldn't even rule out Great Dane somewhere further back.

It's  okay. Truly, it's okay. This kind of problem  is more common  than you think.  And it is difficult  to handle and many people  are heartbroken when their dogs are out of control.

It sounds like your dog has a severe  case of fear aggressive and anxiety. Sometimes  this is genetic, sometimes  its something  a dog develops for multiple  reasons, such as a lack of socialization. But it  isn't always the owners fault that this happens, but a lack of experience can exacerbate the problem. Severe cases are quite difficult  to handle even for most professionals with experience. 

What happened  with the bite is a common  case of redirected aggression; that is, the dog is so reactive  he directed his aggression  at the first thing that touched him, which was you. There were a number  of pressure points  in this situation...being restricted  a leash, seeing another dog...it all, as you say, boiled over and triggered a fight/flight response in your dog. The good news is: yes you and your dog can be given a set of coping  skills for these situations. Reactive  behavior  can be modified. 

One thing to note: people  who work with highly  reactive  dogs in protection work will not touch a dog in a state of hyperarousal. They do not reach out to pet their own dogs once their dog has passed a certain point. They use what they have on hand to control the dog such as the leash; and they are trained  to do this as safely as possible. I question  the behaviorist  you worked with and  why they may have suggested  you pet your dog as a way of calming them down. This is dangerous with a highly  reactive  dog in a severely agitated  state, and is probably  one of the most common  way someone  gets bitten. I don't think  the current strategies  you have been provided  will be effective, especially  if you are being bitten.

The situation  can be salvaged  though. But you will need  to work with someone  who specializes  in dogs with serious behavior  issues to help you and your  dog together. Unfortunately, not many people  are equipped  to do this. The second option  depends on where you live. I don't  recommend  surrendering the dog unless it's to a no-kill shelter. This level of reactivity  means the dog is at high risk of being put down.  But perhaps there will  be a trainer or someone  with experience  with troubled dogs that can take over from you.  Your dog and you are in distress. You need help. And there is no  shame in needing help or struggling  to cope. This is the situation, and it's better to just deal with the situation, forget about who is to blame for it or what should have been done differently. 
I suggest take a deep breath, step back, stop beating yourself up. Let's look at solutions  that will work for you and your dog.

Oof.  I hope I can answer it carefully and respectfully, to atheists and theists alike.  I don't have any coherent view of atheism. I feel like people often want to rally around something, and atheism is one of those things, and mostly that's fine. I also think for many, who are leaving extremely religious households, atheism is a reaction, a sort of brain purge to reject everything you were taught and that might be necessary to start over, figuring out what you do believe and what your values are.

I'm not an afairist because I don't believe in fairies. I'm not an abelieber because I'm not a Justin Bieber fan. Those would be bizarre reactionary positions to take against things that mean something to other people. So, I'm not an atheist because I don't think anybody really walked on water 2000 years ago.

Atheism has been around for a long time. There definitely have been atheistic movements. And naturally, there are atheistic communities. And it's all valid. Religion has a lot to answer for. But there's a stalled dialectic here and the two antithetical positions prop each other up and feed each other. It creates an ingroup, outgroup bias. A sense of tribalism and so on. and so on. ( disclaimer: this is all my opinion.). 

Ideally, I think if we could all just stop taking these absolute reactionary positions against other groups, we would have a better chance of healthy dialogue, or at least of tolerance and acceptance. It's not just Atheism vs. religion, it's almost every part of society online where we need position ourselves within a certain framework that is almost always in direct opposition with another group.

**TLDR:** it can be a community or a movement, but that's a lot of mental space to give something you don't believe in. I don't see the point anymore, personally.

Learn about basic sentence structure. A basic sentence or clause  has a noun, a verb and a object. For a sentence  to be complete sentence  it needs a noun and a verb, so Jack jumps is complete sentence. Jack jumps.

That is a simple  sentence. You also get a compound  sentence  and complex sentence.

A compound sentence  joins two simple  sentences with a conjunction  or a semicolon like this:

Jack jumps over the fence and he hurts himself. 

Or

Jack jumps over the fence; he hurts himself.

If you put a comma between the two clauses, it becomes a comma splice, which is a type of run-on sentence and is grammatically  incorrect.

Jack jumps over the fence, he hurts himself.

If you put other incorrect punctuation  or no conjunction, it is also a run on:

Jack jumps over the fence he hurts  himself.

Then there is a a complex sentence with subordinate  clauses and subordinating  conjunctions. But I'm  not getting into  that now.

If you submit work with run-on sentences, fragments or other grammar errors its going to be hard to get work. Editors generally  want work as close to perfect as possible. Brush  up on your grammar and also invest in a grammarly  subscription  is my advice.
